newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Confidence in HK's rights under threat - Amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Confidence in HK's rights under threat - Amnesty.

text.p: Confidence in Hong Kong is being eroded by mixed signals on human rights from the China-backed leaders who will run the territory after June 30, Amnesty International said on Wednesday.
The independent human rights watchdog urged the territory's future leader Tung Chee-hwa to pledge he would maintain and strengthen safeguards on human rights and back up his promises with action.

"The incoming authorities are fast eroding confidence by sending mixed signals on the critical issue of human rights," Rory Mungoven, Amnesty's Asia and Pacific programme director, told a news conference.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.

While the territory of 6.3 million people has been promised a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover under Sino-British treaties, many fear its freedoms and democratic institutions will be crippled.

One disturbing signal was sent recently in the proposal by a China-appointed body to repeal parts of Hong Kong laws relating to civil liberties, which prompted sharp criticism from the territory's pro-democracy camp as well as Washington and London.
"Some of these proposed changes, if implemented, would risk diluting human rights safeguards in Hong Kong," Mungoven said.
Changes to existing ordinances would make it easier for authorities to ban peaceful demonstrations or non-governmental organisations which are deemed to be undesirable, he said.
Tung and his incoming administration should act to quell such uncertainties, Amnesty said.

"The incoming authorities, including...Mr Tung Chee-hwa, must move quickly to give unequivocal assurances that they will maintain and strengthen safeguards for human rights and back this up with action," Mungoven said.
Public opinion on the transition has been mixed.

A recent government survey found 73 percent of 1,506 respondents were confident post-handover Hong Kong would remain prosperous and stable. But a poll published on Wednesday in the Ming Pao newspaper said 778 residents had downgraded Tung's "ability" and "trustworthiness" since a survey on January 30.

The organisation, which established its Hong Kong office in 1976 and says it is committed to remaining after the handover, said it would push hard in the months ahead for the overseas resettlement of remaining Chinese dissidents in Hong Kong who fear reprisals from Beijing after the transition.
"In the next few months, Amnesty International will need to intensify to help those who remain at risk," Mungoven said.
